en: Itivuttaka 65: Tikanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a dry piece of wood; the person who is like a piece of wood with sap; and the person who is like a piece of wood that is wet. And how, monks, is one a person like a dry piece of wood? Here, monks, a certain person does not pay homage to those worthy of homage, does not rise for those for whom one should rise, does not offer a seat to those for whom one should offer a seat, does not offer water for washing the feet to those for whom one should offer water for washing the feet, and does not show proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. This, monks, is called a person like a dry piece of wood. And how, monks, is one a person like a piece of wood with sap? Here, monks, a certain person pays homage to those worthy of homage, rises for those for whom one should rise, offers a seat to those for whom one should offer a seat, offers water for washing the feet to those for whom one should offer water for washing the feet, and shows proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. Yet he does not listen to the Dhamma, does not attend upon those who teach the Dhamma, does not inquire about the meaning of what has been taught, and does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a person like a piece of wood with sap. And how, monks, is one a person like a piece of wood that is wet? Here, monks, a certain person pays homage to those worthy of homage, rises for those for whom one should rise, offers a seat to those for whom one should offer a seat, offers water for washing the feet to those for whom one should offer water for washing the feet, and shows proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. He listens to the Dhamma, attends upon those who teach the Dhamma, inquires about the meaning of what has been taught, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a person like a piece of wood that is wet. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, it would be good if you were to explain to me the meaning of what was briefly stated by the Blessed One when he rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. “Friend, as for what was briefly stated by the Blessed One, having understood its meaning, I shall explain it to you. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, friend,” the monk replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “The person like a dry piece of wood, friend, is one who does not pay homage to those worthy of homage... and does not show proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. Because of that, he does not gain much wealth, much grain, many possessions, much gold and silver, many wives and children, many male and female slaves, many goats and sheep, many elephants, horses, mules, and cattle, and many fields and lands. When he dies, he goes to an unhappy destination and is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, or in hell. Why is that? Because, friend, this person is devoid of faith, devoid of virtue, devoid of learning, devoid of generosity, and devoid of wisdom. The person like a piece of wood with sap, friend, is one who pays homage to those worthy of homage... and shows proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. Yet he does not listen to the Dhamma, does not attend upon those who teach the Dhamma, does not inquire about the meaning of what has been taught, and does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Because of that, he gains much wealth, much grain, many possessions, much gold and silver, many wives and children, many male and female slaves, many goats and sheep, many elephants, horses, mules, and cattle, and many fields and lands. But when he dies, he goes to an unhappy destination and is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, or in hell. Why is that? Because, friend, although this person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. The person like a piece of wood that is wet, friend, is one who pays homage to those worthy of homage... and shows proper courtesy to those for whom one should show proper courtesy. He listens to the Dhamma, attends upon those who teach the Dhamma, inquires about the meaning of what has been taught, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma. Because of that, he gains much wealth, much grain, many possessions, much gold and silver, many wives and children, many male and female slaves, many goats and sheep, many elephants, horses, mules, and cattle, and many fields and lands. And when he dies, he goes to a happy destination and is reborn in a heavenly world. Why is that? Because, friend, this person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and he practices in accordance with the Dhamma. When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken thus, that monk said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Excellent, friend Ānanda! Excellent, friend Ānanda! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been explained by the Venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, and I go for refuge to the Sangha of Bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge for as long as life lasts.”
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Monks, there are these three kinds of good conduct."
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—
these, monks, are the three kinds of good conduct.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.

This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
